title: Linear-size universal point sets for planar graphs
formal: Does there exist a universal real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), some set \(U_n\subset\mathbb R^2\) of at most \(Cn\) distinct points supports a crossing-free straight-line drawing of every simple planar graph on \(n\) vertices?
why: This asks whether a linear geometric host can represent all planar combinatorial structures of a given size, rather than dedicating a separate layout to each graph.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. Gordon’s new preprint claims n^{1+o(1)} universal point sets for general planar graphs, but does not state the fixed-constant linear bound requested here. The new proof has not been independently verified. No proof or refutation of the O(n) target was located in the bounded source search.

progress.text: Linear-size constructions for restricted planar graph classes do not establish a universal linear bound for all planar graphs.
Gordon’s preprint claims an unrestricted \(n^{1+o(1)}\) upper bound. This is not a constant-factor linear bound, and the proof has not been independently verified in this pass.

definitions: The point set \(U_n\) is chosen as a function of \(n\) before the graph is supplied. For each finite simple undirected planar graph \(G\) with vertex set \([n]\), there must be an injective map \(\phi:V(G)\to U_n\). Every edge is drawn as the closed line segment between its endpoint images. Two edge segments may intersect only at the image of a shared endpoint, and the relative interior of an edge may contain no vertex image. Unused points in \(U_n\) are allowed. The injection may depend on \(G\); the same prescribed correspondence of labels to points is not required. The graph need not have a prescribed planar embedding. Coordinates are arbitrary reals, and no grid-size, computability or runtime constraint is imposed. A planar graph means one admitting a plane embedding by arcs with these same incidence and nonintersection requirements.

context_blocks.text: A universal point set is chosen before the graph is known. Once a graph arrives, its vertices may be assigned to any suitable distinct points of that same set. The question is whether a constant number of available points per graph vertex always suffices for every planar graph of that size.

Location matters even for four vertices. The complete graph on four vertices is planar, but putting all four vertices on the corners of a convex quadrilateral forces its two diagonals to cross. A planar straight-line drawing can instead place one vertex inside the triangle formed by the other three. Thus a large collection of points in convex position is not by itself universal for planar graphs.

Classical straight-line grid-drawing theorems give a universal \(O(n)\)-by-\(O(n)\) grid and therefore \(O(n^2)\) available points. Lower bounds exceeding \(n\) show that using exactly one point per vertex is too restrictive in general, but a constant-factor lower bound does not refute the existence of some larger universal linear constant.

The 2023 work gives linear-size sets for restricted classes of planar graphs. A host set for a class with additional structural constraints need not support all planar graphs. This is why the quantified graph family, as well as the number of points, is part of the target.

A preprint posted on 10 September 2026 claims universal sets of size \(n^{1+o(1)}\) for unrestricted planar graphs. This improves the stated general upper frontier if its proof is correct, but it does not assert \(Cn\) for a fixed constant. For example, \(n\log n\) also has the form \(n^{1+o(1)}\) while its ratio to \(n\) is unbounded. The preprint’s claim is recorded without an independent proof audit.

The input graph has no prescribed embedding or fixed correspondence between vertex labels and host points. Coordinates may be arbitrary real numbers. Allowing a bend in each edge, prescribing the vertex-to-point assignment, or requiring a small integer grid would change the existence question.

answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that a constant \(C>0\) and sets \(U_n\) with the stated universal drawing property exist for every \(n\), or prove the logical negation in Lean: for every \(C>0\), some \(n\) has the property that every point set of size at most \(Cn\) fails to support at least one simple planar graph on \(n\) vertices. The point set precedes the graph in the quantifiers, and each successful drawing may choose its own vertex assignment.
